title: The Gambler's Fallacy: When 'Due' Is an Illusion

body.heading: The night the wheel went black
paragraphs: In August 1913, at the Monte Carlo Casino, a roulette ball landed on black 26 times in a row. As the streak grew, gamblers crowded the table betting on red, certain it was due. They lost fortunes. Every spin, including the 27th, was an independent event - the wheel had no memory of the streak and no debt to repay.

This mistake is called the gambler's fallacy: believing that past random events change the odds of the next one. A coin that has landed heads five times is not 'due' for tails. It is just a coin, and the next flip is still fifty-fifty.

body.heading: What the law of large numbers really says
paragraphs: People often defend the fallacy with a real law: in the long run, heads and tails do balance out to about half each. But the balance arrives by dilution, not by correction. A streak of five heads gets swamped by thousands of later flips; the coin never compensates, it just gets outnumbered.

There is a mirror-image mistake too: the hot-hand fallacy, believing a streak means the next success is more likely. In pure chance games, both beliefs are wrong in opposite directions. The honest summary is boring and powerful: independent events stay independent.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Keep a prediction journal for one evening of any game involving dice, cards or coins. Before each random event, write your prediction and, honestly, whether a streak influenced it. Afterwards, count how often 'due' thinking appeared - and how it performed.
You will probably find the urge to bet against a streak is strongest exactly when it is least justified. Noticing the urge, rather than obeying it, is the real skill this fallacy teaches.

takeaway: Independent events don't remember: after any streak, the next flip is still fifty-fifty.
